newsitem.title: UK: Journalists barred from UK nurses trial in Saudi.
newsitem.headline: Journalists barred from UK nurses trial in Saudi.

text.p: Journalists will not be able to attend the trial of two British nurses facing a possible death penalty over the alleged murder of a colleague in Saudi Arabia, the Saudi embassy in London said on Saturday.
An embassy statement said that the two women, who say they are not guilty, will get a fair trial when the court case resumes on Sunday after a three-week break.
It added that the death penalty would only be considered if the court found "incontrovertible evidence of premeditated murder."

Lucille McLaughlan, 31, and Deborah Parry, 38, deny murdering Australian nurse Yvonne Gilford at the King Fahd medical centre in Dhahran last December. They say they were pressured into making false statements admitting the crime.
Under Saudi law, relatives of Gilford are entitled to express a preference for so called "blood money" or execution if the two women are found guilty.

In a series of media interviews Gilford's brother Frank has indicated that he would seek the death penalty in the case, which has riveted media in both Australia and Britain and brought calls for a more open, public trial.

The Saudi embassy statement said it had received several media requests to attend the trial but went on: "There is no precedent in our judicial history of journalists being allowed into a courtroom, and the Saudi Government does not intend to change this rule in this case."
Clarifying Saudi law, the statement said that it was up to the victim's family to demand "retribution" - but it was for the court, not relatives, to determine guilt.
"Only if the court determines that capital punishment is the appropriate sentence would the court ask the victim's family if they wished to demand or waive the sentence," it said.
The term blood money was misleading and should instead be interpreted as "compensation for manslaughter", said the embassy.
It said that the court's verdict was only the "first stage" of a trial, and if capital punishment were involved the cause would automatically go on to a five-judge appeal court.
The case would then be subject to review by another court and finally the king in a process that could take between one and two years.
